posts.caption: A family pulled over on the county road yesterday and climbed out with their phones already up. The little boy wanted to know if the big red horse was friendly. I was standing at the gate with a bucket in each hand, so I said she's friendly if you're holding a carrot. They did not have a carrot. Big Red looked at them for a long minute, then walked off to the shade tree like a woman leaving a meeting that ran over. The boy waved anyway. She flicked one ear, which for her is a full parade wave.
posts.first: My first draft horse was a gelding named Duke who greeted every stranger like a long lost cousin. I assumed all big horses were like that. Then I bought Big Red. She has opinions about visitors, delivery trucks, and the color of my truck. I've learned to introduce people to her slowly and from the side.

posts.caption: The wind took a grocery bag off the neighbor's trash can around seven this morning and delivered it to our paddock fence. By seven-ten the small pony had located it. By seven-fifteen he'd announced it to the whole barn, in the whinny he usually saves for a stray dog. I walked out in my slippers to inspect it. It was an empty bag from the feed store with a coupon stuck to the bottom. Pudding watched from behind the water trough with only his forelock showing. I put the bag in the bin. He has not forgiven the bin.
posts.first: The winter I got Pudding I tried to desensitize him to tarps. I laid one in the aisle and he walked around it for three weeks. On day twenty-two he stepped right on it, looked at me, and went back to eating. We have never spoken of it. The bag is a different matter entirely.

Text at the top reads: Field report: a plastic bag has been in the paddock since morning. I have filed it under predators.

posts.quote: The barn cat has moved to the top of the hay stack and now looks down on the horses. Everyone can feel the difference.
posts.first: The cat has been up there since Monday. I've stopped climbing for the top bale and started using the lower ones, out of respect. The horses watch her from the aisle and say nothing. The hay man stacked it, and he has taken no responsibility.

posts.caption: The yearling came in September, all legs and opinions, and attached himself to the oldest gelding on the property by the second day. Now he stands where the gray horse stands, drinks when he drinks, and cocks one hip at the fence like he's been doing it for twenty years. The old gelding pretends not to notice. I've watched him, though. He squares up a little when the little one is looking. He also keeps the good sunny spot for himself, which I suspect is a lesson of its own.
posts.first: My grandfather kept a black mare until she was thirty-one. By the end the younger horses followed her to every gate. He used to say you never find out who's watching you until you try to do something small and right. I think about that when I fill the water trough.

posts.caption: Fall shots day always starts the same way. I park the truck at the end of the barn aisle and stack the paperwork on the mounting block, and every horse on the property suddenly gets very interested in the back corner of the stall. The vet came down the line with his bag. At stall four he stopped, looked over the half door, and kept walking toward the goat pen. The round bay mare stared after him for a long moment. Then she sighed, rearranged the cat, and went back to her hay. I think she's been rehearsing for that visit since August.
posts.first: I always dread the vet's visits more than the horses do. This one brought his daughter along, about nine, who walked the whole aisle naming every horse she met and asking each one how they were feeling. The mare in stall four let her pet her nose for ten minutes. That never happens for me.

posts.caption: The feed store wanted pictures for their barn calendar, so I spent an hour brushing a chestnut mare until she shone like a new penny. I braided a section of mane. I wiped the dust off her face with a damp cloth. She posed like she'd done this before, which she has, according to her. The photographer took eleven shots. I picked the one where she's mid-sneeze, because it was the only honest one. It goes up on the feed store wall for March. The mare has taken it better than I have.
posts.first: She sneezed because I put too much shine spray on her forelock. I'd meant to wipe it off and forgot. She turned her head, gave me a look, and held it until the photographer finished. I've agreed to be more careful with the spray. She has not agreed to forget the sneeze.
